Veterinary medicine · published research

Canine elbow osteoarthritis

In 20 dogs with naturally occurring elbow osteoarthritis, nine of 11 PBM-treated dogs reduced NSAID use compared with none of nine sham-treated dogs. Blinded assessments also favored PBM for lameness and pain after nine treatments over six weeks.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In 20 dogs with naturally occurring elbow osteoarthritis, nine of 11 PBM-treated dogs reduced NSAID use compared with none of nine sham-treated dogs. Blinded assessments also favored PBM for lameness and pain after nine treatments over six weeks.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Joints > Osteoarthritis elbow mapping contains one primary veterinary clinical trial. It enrolled client-owned dogs with naturally occurring elbow osteoarthritis rather than an induced laboratory model. Broader canine osteoarthritis papers on hip or mixed joints are not counted as direct elbow evidence.

Human and clinical evidence

No human elbow-osteoarthritis study is relevant to this canine indication. Looney et al. randomized 20 dogs with naturally occurring elbow osteoarthritis to PBM or sham, with 11 in the active group and nine in the sham group. Nine active-treatment dogs reduced their nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, compared with none in the sham group. Blinded personnel also recorded better lameness and pain scores in the active group after nine treatments over six weeks (2018). This is one small trial, not a replicated treatment program.

Animal evidence

The study is clinical veterinary evidence from naturally affected client-owned dogs, not an induced animal model. No other elbow-specific animal experiment is listed.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell, tissue, or ex-vivo study is listed for canine elbow osteoarthritis.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trial used a multimodal laser device applied to the elbows over nine sessions across six weeks. The paper reports cumulative fluence of 10 to 20 J/cm2 depending on dog size. Wavelength is the light's color band and affects tissue penetration. This protocol cannot be assumed to apply to other joints, devices, or species.

Interpretation

The trial supports a possible improvement in pain, lameness, and medication use for naturally affected dogs. Its small sample, single study group, and limited replication leave the size and durability of benefit uncertain. Independent elbow-specific trials should report device settings and validated owner and clinician outcomes.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for improved pain, lameness, and reduced NSAID use in one blinded canine elbow trial Very low for replication, optimal dose, or application to other joints or species
Publications and records1 title (exact elbow-specific veterinary category)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small randomized placebo-controlled study in 20 naturally affected dogs reported lower lameness and pain scores and reduced NSAID use. It has not been independently replicated for elbow osteoarthritis. A larger trial should prespecify owner and clinician outcomes, report dose clearly, and assess long-term function.
